So I'm curious as to what's your understanding of CCP's infiltration into the U.S. media, into the U.S. education system, into the U.S. justice system?
Oh, man.
I mean, you know, any topic, any topic, any institution, every institution is being dominated by this.
I remember Newt Gingrich was on a Fox News interview with Harris Faulkner, and he mentioned the name George Soros.
And, you know, the producers went nuts, and, you know, the thing in her ear is you can't talk.
He said, what, is that name now verboten?
Well, all of this stuff is in the universities, in the media, and the taboo on not talking about the subjects, yet the changing of the language for the stuff that you can talk about.
They're trying to change our culture, their culture, every culture, to be this Marxist, communist, evil, satanic force in the world that we can't afford to have running amongst us.
Dr. Redfield, did you agree, in your opinion, with Dr. Anderson's assessment at the time that this virus did look engineered?
I was concerned because of the presence of the furin cleavage site that we've talked about.
And I think it's important to understand what that cleavage site does.
That cleavage site totally changes the orientation of the binding domain of COVID.
So it now, which could not see the ACE2 receptor, which is the human receptor, it totally changes the orientation now.
So it has high affinity for a human receptor.
So that furin cleavage site bothered me.
It didn't seem that it belonged there.
And then when you look at the sequences that it used, and it's beyond the committee, but I know many of you have looked into it,
the sequences that they used in those 12 nucleotides for arginine were the arginine sequences nucleotide triplet that coded for the human arginine.
So why did this virus have the arginine sequences for human there, not bat?
It was very disconcerting to me.
It looked like this virus was engineered.
Was this, what you're observing and speaking of, is this something that would be in line with gain-of-function research
and the capabilities it would provide to the virus?
Yeah.
I mean, basically this lab published in 2014 that they accomplished in this, allowing the coronaviruses that they were working with in the lab to bind to the ACE2 receptor and humanize mice.
And the only way they did that was by reorienting the binding domain.
And it was clear to them at this time that that was likely the issue in their private conversations.
Yet by February 4th, a paper on the origins of COVID is drafted by four participants of the February 1 conference call.
One of those participants, Dr. Anderson, completely reverses himself in an email to the president of EcoHealth, Peter Dozik,
and says the main crackpot theories going around at the moment relate to this virus being somehow engineered.
And that is demonstrably false.
My question to you, Mr. Redfield, did you know of any evidence that they had found within three days from February 1st to February 4th
to be able to confirm that it was not created in a lab?
As I mentioned earlier, unfortunately I was excluded from those conversations,
which I found retroactively very disappointed, since I was obviously a virologist and very engaged.
and I actually had asked Jeremy Farrar, Tony Fauci, and Ted Rose to have these conversations.
And then to be excluded, I found unusual.
I do think it illustrates one point that's worth really focusing on.
When you have a group of people that decide there could only be one point of view, that's problematic.
And I'll keep going saying it's antithetical to science.
And unfortunately that's what they did.
I will say if you go back and look, it's declassified now.
And I'm sure you all have your classified briefings.
But the declassified information now, in September of 2019, three things happened in that lab.
One is they deleted the sequences.
It was highly irregular.
Researchers don't usually like to do that.
Second thing they did was they changed the command and control of the lab from the civilian control to the military control.
Highly unusual.
And I've been involved in dual-use labs when I was in the military.
And the third thing they did, which I think is really telling,
is they led a contract to redo the ventilation system in that laboratory.
So I think clearly there was strong evidence that there was a significant event that happened in that laboratory in September.
It's now been declassified.
You can read it.
I'm sure there's more classified information around.
The most downloaded app in the world, one of the most downloaded apps in the world,
the social media company, TikTok.
Could the Chinese government, through its ownership of ByteDance, that owns ByteDance U.S.,
if they wanted to and ByteDance U.S. were willing to cooperate or forced to cooperate,
could they use TikTok to control data on millions of users?
Yes.
Could they use it to control the software on millions of devices, given the opportunity to do so?
Yes.
Could they use it to drive narratives, like to divide Americans against each other?
For example, let's say China wants to invade Taiwan, to make sure that Americans are seeing videos arguing why Taiwan belongs to China,
why the U.S. should not intervene?
Yes.
And I would make the point on that last one in particular,
that we're not sure that we would see many of the outward signs of it happening if it was happening.
And I think the thing that the most fundamental piece that cuts across every one of those risks and threats that you mentioned,
that I think Americans need to understand, is that something that's very sacred in our country,
the difference between the private sector and the public sector,
that's a line that is non-existent in the way the CCP operates.
This is a substantial national security threat for the country of a kind that we didn't face in the past.
So we're still, it's, at the end of the day, it's not about, you know,
some grown man in the middle of the day putting up videos, you know,
that people that have a job shouldn't be putting up.
But it's also about all these other things that we've talked about, the data,
the ability to manipulate information.
I would imagine that it's probably one of the most valuable surveillance tools on the planet.
I mean, if we went out and decided to build something like this of our own,
to influence or spy on another society, I'm not sure we could build something like this or even better.
And we've invited them in and protected them by our laws.
So I don't understand why this company is allowed to operate.
Now, look, speaking of defence, The Age and the Sydney Morning Herald this morning
are running an important and timely discussion on the real prospects of war on our doorstep.
Now, sure, China's not going to invade Australia anytime soon.
But China doesn't actually need to invade us.
If the United States is defeated and driven out of the Western Pacific,
unless Australia were prepared to turn itself into an antipodean Israel
with conscription and even nuclear weapons,
we would effectively become an economic colony of China,
producing food and minerals for the motherland.
Think back to the 14 demands published by the Chinese embassy just two years ago.
We had to accept, they said, all Chinese investment,
accept all Chinese students,
make no criticisms of Chinese government policy
and break our defence alliance with the US.
We're all aware, or should be,
of the Beijing government's determination to take Taiwan
by force if necessary, Taiwan in practical terms,
an independent island democracy of 24 million people
that at no other time in its history
has ever been ruled by communist Beijing.
We should all be aware too of Beijing's often declared aim
to be the world's top power by mid-century.
Now, why is that any business of ours?
Well, if one island democracy of 24 million people
can be gobbled up by a bully neighbour,
why not another,
given all the natural resources we have that China wants
and our capacity to feed a billion people,
should it ever come to that?
Then there's the disruption that any attack on Taiwan would bring,
not just in spiking of oil and gas prices,
as we've seen with the energy drought in Europe
caused by the Ukraine war,
but in the case of a Sino conflict,
the complete cessation of shipping
through the South East China Seas
and the East China Seas,
that carry something like 50% of the world's maritime trade.
And in just the area of technology alone,
the loss of 70% of the world's semiconductors,
those little items are now in almost everything,
well, they're made in Taiwan.
If the US fails to defend Taiwan,
the whole US alliance system will collapse.
If the US does defend Taiwan,
it's war between superpowers,
the very thing that the Ukraine war so far
has been managed carefully to avoid.
If we should have learned one thing from Ukraine,
it's that you come into any conflict
with the arms you have now.
Once the fighting starts,
it's too late to ramp up arms manufacture
to acquire new weapons and train first-class soldiers.
If there's one thing that Beijing would have learned itself from Ukraine,
it's that the West's stocks of arms and ammunition
have already run dangerously low to supply one conflict,
let alone two.
So this is a perilous time.
Xi Jinping has reportedly told his generals
to be ready to invade Taiwan within five years.
One US admiral has said it could happen within a year.
This is what makes the imminent forced posture review
by the federal government so critical.
It would be almost impossible for us to remain a US ally
and stand aside from any democracy versus dictatorship fight.
So we need to be as ready as we can be.
And our government in Canberra needs to be upfront with Australians
about how serious these considerations are
so that we all understand what's in contemplation here and in Beijing.
And China needs to know in blunt terms
that only autocrats understand
that we're as ready as we can be
because there's only strength that deters aggression.
and continued deterrence is what's needed
if the unthinkable is to remain unlikely.

And so tell me, since we have this new Congress,
what's the percentage of your work is about CCP or China,

it's the CCP.

the government, the Congress, and what's been happening.

they're very, very concerned.

is I ask everyday Americans, what do they think, right?
What do they think?
Most of the people on the street
seem to have a very, very disconnected view of China.
They don't seem to think that China is a very big threat.
They think they make a lot of things
and they provide our country with a lot of things.
But I would say the average American
is waking up to the fact that the CCP
and Jiang Jinping in general are nefarious in nature.
I'm not going to go into COVID here
because we all know about that.
but if you need a liver at the NIH
and let's say you're a celebrity and you have money,
the wait is four years.
If you need a liver in China
and you have the money, perfect match.
Now, where is that coming from?
That's what people have to ask themselves.
And the more things we discover about Jiang Jinping
and his regime,
the more that it seems like America
is almost destined to war with China
and no one wants this.
Yeah, absolutely.
And you're raising a very important question.
Why America is doing business
with such a regime
that commits the human rights atrocity,
like killing people for their organs?
And another thing you talk about,
the people in the strait,
they probably don't have much understanding
about why CCP is a big threat.

because pretty much the CCP owned them.
The CCP has spending tens of millions of dollars
influencing and buying America's mainstream media.
And we didn't have the real America voice years ago.
Now we have it.
And we all know the reasons why, right?
Well, people are waking up exactly.
And the goods that China provides this country with are...
